Direct-acting (also called direct-acting or instantaneous) electric radiators convert the electrical energy they draw into heat with essentially 100 percent efficiency at the point of use: every kilowatt-hour of electricity becomes heat in the room. However, when assessing their overall “real-world” efficiency, two further factors must be taken into account:

1. Primary-energy efficiency of electricity generation and delivery  
   • If the electricity comes from low-loss, renewable sources (wind, solar, hydro), the system-level efficiency remains high and greenhouse-gas emissions are very low.  
   • If the electricity is generated from fossil fuels, overall efficiency from primary energy to delivered electricity can be on the order of 30–40 percent once generation and transmission losses are included. Here are several key strategies for improving a house’s natural ventilation. These principles rely on wind‐driven and buoyancy-driven (stack-effect) airflow, and can be combined for best results:

1. Orient and size openings for cross-ventilation  
   • Place intake openings (windows or vents) on the windward side and exhaust openings on the leeward side.  
   • Aim for at least two openings in each primary living space, so air can flow straight through.  
   • Keep the inlet slightly larger than the outlet (or vice versa) to control flow direction and rate.

2. Exploit the stack effect  
   • Install high-level vents or operable clerestory windows toward the top of the room or roof ridge. Warm air rises and will draw cooler air in through lower openings.

Load balancing in the context of electric-vehicle (EV) charging refers to any method or system that ensures the total electrical capacity available at a site is shared intelligently among multiple chargers or charging points. Its purpose is to prevent circuit overloads, avoid costly grid-connection upgrades and make the best use of the existing electrical infrastructure.

In Sweden, stairwells are normally classified as “unheated common parts” in the building regulations. According to Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR 26, chapter 6:12), the air temperature in such spaces must not fall below 12 °C. This minimum:

• prevents frost and condensation in the structure and installations  
• satisfies the absolute requirement for health and safety  

If you require a higher level of comfort (for example in public‐access buildings, care facilities or in stairwells used frequently), BBR refers to the thermal‐comfort standard SS-EN ISO 7730, which recommends maintaining 16–18 °C in areas where people spend short periods.

Ventilation balancing is the process of adjusting a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that the supply and exhaust airflow rates in each room or zone match the design intent. In other words, it ensures that every space receives just the right amount of fresh air and that exhaust air is removed at the correct rate. Although exact energy savings depend on how unbalanced a system was to begin with and on the building’s characteristics, the following points summarize the general energy-use impacts of proper ventilation balancing:

1. Prevents over-ventilation (General guidance)  
   • If some rooms receive more supply air than they need, the HVAC system must heat or cool that excess air—wasting energy. Balancing dampers and fans to design flows avoids this unnecessary load.

2. Reduces air-leakage losses (General guidance)  
   • Unbalanced systems create positive or negative pressures, which drive uncontrolled infiltration (winter) or exfiltration (summer) through cracks and gaps
